html:
Nunavik is the Inuit homeland of northern Quebec, the land north of the 55th parallel between Hudson Bay and Ungava Bay. Almost all of its 14,000 people live in fourteen villages on the coast, and about nine in ten are Inuit.

Before the Inuit, the Dorset people lived here. The Thule, ancestors of today's Inuit, arrived from the west after about 1200 and replaced them. In 1492 Inuit families moved between coastal camps, hunting seals, walrus, whales and caribou with kayaks, dog sleds and harpoons. The Innu lived in the forests to the south.

The Hudson's Bay Company opened trading posts here from the 1800s, and missions and government settlements followed in the 1900s. When Quebec began huge hydro dams in the north, the Inuit and Cree signed the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975, which gave Nunavik its own regional government. Like Nunatsiavut in Labrador, it is part of Inuit Nunangat, the Inuit lands of Canada.
